28 A wave on the surface of water passes through a gap between two barriers and is diffracted, as
shown.
barrier
barrier
What happens when the frequency of the wave is halved?
A
Less diffraction is observed.
B
More diffraction is observed.
C
There is no diffraction.
D
The same amount of diffraction is observed.

hints: Notice the fixed gap width between the two barriers and that only the frequency is changed to half its value.
Recall $v = f\lambda$ for water waves at constant depth, so halving $f$ with constant $v$ must change $\lambda$.
Connect the new $\lambda$ to the rule that diffraction is greatest when $\lambda$ is comparable to or larger than the gap width.
walkthrough: Identify the setup: plane water wavefronts pass through a narrow gap and spread into curved wavefronts, which is diffraction.
State the governing relation $v = f\lambda$. In the same water the speed $v$ is unchanged.
Halving the frequency gives $\lambda = v/f$, so the new wavelength is twice the old wavelength: $\lambda_{new} = 2\lambda_{old}$.
Recall the diffraction rule: the amount of spreading increases as the ratio of wavelength to gap width increases, with maximum spreading when gap width is about $\lambda$.
Since $\lambda$ is larger and closer to the gap width, the transmitted wavefronts curve round more strongly. This is option B.

A.explanation: Halving frequency increases wavelength, so spreading increases rather than decreases.

B.explanation: Longer wavelength is closer to the gap width, so the wave spreads out more after the barriers.

C.explanation: Diffraction still occurs at a gap; changing frequency changes the amount of spreading, not whether it exists.

D.explanation: The wavelength changes when frequency changes, so the ratio of wavelength to gap width and the diffraction change.
